column1: Mimicking

Can you describe the smelliest person you have met? It was a sweltering Tuesday in early August, and I was waiting for the 2:45 bus at the corner of High Street and Elm. The heat was oppressive, the air thick with humidity, and the scent of overripe garbage wafted from the overflowing bins nearby. This was the usual olfactory onslaught of a typical summer afternoon in the city, and I, in my youthful naïveté, believed myself prepared for it. I was wrong. As the bus lumbered into view, a figure emerged from the crowded shelter. He was a man of middle age, clad in a stained, oversized trench coat that appeared to have seen better decades. His face was obscured by a greasy, unkempt mop of hair, and he clutched a tattered plastic bag that seemed to be overflowing with… something. As he approached, I braced myself, expecting the standard summer-afternoon cityscape smells of hot asphalt and exhaust fumes. Instead, I was hit by a wave of pure, concentrated stench so potent it nearly knocked me off my feet. It was a rancid, acrid odor, a symphony of the putrid - a blend of unwashed body, stale cigarettes, and something else entirely, something indefinable yet undeniably foul. It clung to the air, a suffocating miasma that seemed to emanate from every pore of this unfortunate individual. The bus doors hissed open, the other passengers seemingly oblivious, except for a young woman who gave me the shared look of disgust. The man shuffled onto the bus, his trench coat billowing around him, and secured himself a seat towards the back. I boarded the bus, holding my breath, and prayed the next stop would arrive quickly.

What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? The most unprofessional thing a doctor ever said to me wasn't exactly a groundbreaking revelation, but it struck me at the time with the force of a poorly aimed, albeit ineffective, slap. It was during a routine check-up when I was about seventeen, a young lad grappling with the usual teenage angst and the general complexities of existence. The doctor, a man who looked like he’d seen more years than seasons, casually glanced at my medical records, and with a voice that held the same warmth as a Monday morning, he declared, "Son, based on your history, you're a hypochondriac alright." Now, I wasn't exactly thrilled with the assessment. I mean, everyone's a little dramatic about their health when they're seventeen, right? A cough could signal the end of days, a headache, the precursor to a brain tumor. But to have a medical professional, someone I was entrusting with my well-being, essentially label me as a drama queen, well, it was, let’s say, less than ideal. He didn’t offer any further explanation, or suggestion, no words of comfort. Just a flat statement.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? I've always found that question rather perplexing. The supposed animosity feels like one of those tired tropes, a caricature perpetuated more by wishful thinking and insecurity than any grounded reality. It's the kind of question that gets thrown around with the same dismissive energy as "Why do all men only want one thing?" or "Why can't women just be more feminine?". I suspect the truth is far more nuanced, far less easily packaged into a pithy, inflammatory statement. What does “nerdy” even encompass these days? Is it the guy engrossed in quantum physics, the one sketching elaborate fantasy worlds, the software developer burning the midnight oil, or the gamer glued to his console? The term has become so broad and diluted, I often wonder if it even holds any real meaning anymore. Some women might not find certain traits appealing, sure. But to paint an entire gender as harboring unadulterated *hate* for another based on their interests or intellectual inclinations seems absurd to me.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? I’m no film critic, but I’ve certainly made my judgments. Call it a guilty pleasure, maybe even a character flaw, but I'll openly admit to assessing movies based solely on their posters. The one that springs to mind is a predictable, cliché-ridden rom-com, the kind that clogs up the cinema listings every other week. You know the type: sickly-sweet title in a bubbly font, two impossibly attractive leads gazing into each other’s eyes against a backdrop of vibrant, unrealistic scenery. Sometimes they’re on a beach, sometimes strolling through a park, perpetually bathed in golden hour light. The poster is the cinematic equivalent of a sugar rush – initially appealing, but ultimately leaving you feeling empty and vaguely nauseous. Another offender is the action movie that relies entirely on explosions and testosterone. The poster usually features a muscle-bound protagonist brandishing a ridiculously oversized weapon, silhouetted against a fiery inferno. The tagline will invariably promise “unleashed fury” or some other equally hyperbolic claim. The whole thing screams “style over substance,” and my brain screams, “Avoid!” It’s not just posters, though. The trailer offers the same condensed and often misleading presentation. The trailer for one movie I always refused to watch had a man in a suit fighting other people. So boring.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? It was a balmy Saturday afternoon, the sun casting long shadows across the emerald green lawn of our home. I, a young boy, was perched precariously upon the sturdy branches of the ancient mango tree that had stood sentinel over our house for decades. From my vantage point, the world seemed to unfold in slow motion – the lazy drift of cumulus clouds across the azure canvas of the sky, the gentle buzzing of bees flitting from flower to flower, the rhythmic thump of a cricket ball meeting a wooden bat in the distance. It was, in short, a picture of idyllic childhood. My older sister, a rather precocious teenager, was sprawled out on a deck chair, engrossed in a tattered paperback novel, her brow furrowed in concentration. This was unusual, as she usually preferred gossiping on the phone or applying copious amounts of makeup. My dad, a man of routine, was meticulously tending to his prized vegetable patch, his brow perpetually creased in a look of intense focus. My mom, usually the orchestrator of chaos and the life of the party, was inexplicably quiet, sitting by the poolside and staring into the distance. Suddenly, as though on cue, a storm of unprecedented ferocity descended upon us; the skies turned an ominous shade of gray, the wind howled like a banshee, and the heavens unleashed a torrential downpour. The storm, though formidable, was not the lowest probability event. It was the ensuing happening that defied all logic and probability. A bolt of lightning, seemingly drawn to the mango tree like a moth to a flame, struck it with the force of a thousand suns. The tree, our beloved and venerable companion, instantly erupted in flames. But then, amidst the chaos and the raging inferno, a single, perfect mango, still green and unripe, detached itself from a burning branch and fell directly into my lap. It was as though the heavens themselves had conspired to deposit a small, albeit inedible, token of absurdity and improbability into my unsuspecting hands. The odds of such an event were astronomical, a statistical anomaly that still defies explanation to this day. I sat there frozen, cradling the fiery fruit, dumbfounded by the pure, unadulterated weirdness of it all.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? The question of whether Imane Khelif, a biologically male boxer, should be allowed to compete in the Women's Boxing event at the upcoming Paris Olympics is a sticky wicket, isn’t it? On the one hand, you have the compelling argument of fairness, of preserving the integrity of women's sports. It's hard to deny the inherent physical advantages that a male body possesses – greater muscle mass, bone density, and, let's be candid, raw power. Allowing a male-bodied individual to compete against women in a contact sport like boxing raises serious questions about the safety and competitive balance of the event. It’s not just about winning but about the potential for serious physical harm to the female athletes who are, frankly, at a biological disadvantage. Then you have the other side of the coin, the complex and often fraught terrain of inclusivity and gender identity. We live in an era where understanding and acceptance of transgender and non-binary individuals is becoming increasingly important. Banning a person from participating in the sport they love because of their gender identity, especially after they've met the required biological and performance standards, feels inherently unjust. Where do we draw the line? Do we allow them to compete but implement stricter rules regarding physical contact, weight classes, or other factors in terms of fairness? Do we create a separate category altogether? I can only imagine what kind of heated discussions would be heard throughout the corridors; arguments and counterarguments, personal biases, political agendas and the like. There isn’t an easy answer, and any decision made will likely be met with controversy and debate. It's a situation that demands nuance, empathy, and a relentless pursuit of fairness for all athletes involved. It's a problem not only for boxing, but for any sport.

Has your friend ever saved your life? No, not exactly, but my pal, Kevin, came pretty darn close. It wasn't a matter of fists or bullets, but more a case of a near-miss culinary catastrophe. We were both university students back in the day, sharing a cramped, mold-infested apartment that could barely be called a living space – more like a breeding ground for questionable fungi. Finances were tight, ramen noodles were a staple, and anything remotely resembling a balanced meal was considered a luxury. One evening, fuelled by cheap beer and a desperate craving for something other than the usual gut-busting fare, we decided to get ambitious. We’d cook a proper chicken curry from scratch.Well, the attempt was more disastrous than we could have ever anticipated. We started out reasonably well, following some poorly-written recipe we found online. We struggled cooking everything. That curry was going to be legendary. Then, disaster struck. Some accident with the bottle of chili, all the chilis poured into the pot. The smell of that curry was so bad. My eyes started watering with a deep sense of pain and agony. Kevin started coughing, yelling at me to get out while attempting to put out the curry. This kitchen was hell. The worst part of that incident, was the absolute agony. When there's too much chili, your mind goes through a whole new dimension of agony. We ran out of the apartment and into the pouring rain outside, clutching our stinging eyes and gasping for breath. The whole building was engulfed in the smell of a thousand chilis, with neighbours yelling and banging on doors, while we could only gasp in agony and breathe. Had we not run out of the apartment, which was a one-room area with very little ventilation, we would have eventually succumbed to the fumes and potentially suffocated. So, while Kevin didn’t exactly pull me from a burning building or deflect a bullet, he did save me from what could have been a spicy, torturous, and quite possibly fatal, end. I always keep in my mind that without him, I might not be here at all.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? I certainly have, though I wouldn't call it a "life-changing" experience in the grandiose sense. More accurately, it was a formative one, a lesson learned amidst the steam of the fryers and the relentless buzz of the drive-thru. This happened years ago, when I was a callow youth, barely old enough to shave, and slinging burgers at a popular chain restaurant. The monotony was crushing. The repetitive tasks, the demanding customers, the ever-present stench of grease – it all threatened to suffocate any flicker of creativity or ambition within me. My only respite was the camaraderie, the shared struggles and inside jokes forged in the crucible of the late-night rush. But on this particular Tuesday, something occurred that jarred me from my teenage ennui. A customer, a woman of advanced years, with a severe but kind face, ordered a simple meal. As I was preparing it, I noticed she fumbled with her purse, clearly struggling. Without a word, I handed her a pre-made order ready to go. I had never had to do this before in my job as a cashier and frankly, the manager would’ve killed me for it. But something in her eyes compelled me to. She smiled, a rare and genuine smile which immediately pierced through my otherwise cynical defenses. "Young man," she said, her voice raspy with age, "that was extraordinarily kind of you." And for the first time in my life, I understood the value of a simple, selfless act.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? There are several movies that could have transcended their mediocrity simply by having a more robust screenplay, but this one invariably springs to mind: *The Island of Dr. Moreau.* The film's initial premise—a scientist driven to create human-animal hybrids on a remote island—already possesses the necessary ingredients for a thought-provoking narrative. Yet, the execution flounders almost immediately. One can easily see the potential for a suspenseful, philosophical examination of the ethical boundaries of scientific progress. Imagine a narrative that delved deeper into the psychology of the hybrids, exploring their struggle with their dual nature, or scrutinizing the moral degeneration of the protagonist Dr. Moreau, as he spiraled into madness, losing his sense of humanity. But instead, the screenplay devolves into a disjointed series of confusing events, with stilted dialogue, and uninspired characters. The pacing feels erratic, the plot points lack cohesion, and character motivations are murky at best. Marlon Brando’s performance, though eccentric by design, feels more like performance art rather than a portrayal, his mumbling and improvised lines further detracting from, rather than adding to any tension. If only the movie had opted for character-driven conflicts and a richer exploration of the themes embedded within it, then *The Island of Dr. Moreau* could have been a true classic, etching itself into the cinematic consciousness instead of its now-infamous reputation.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? That's easy, without any doubt whatsoever, it's the ending of *2001: A Space Odyssey*. Stanley Kubrick, the master of cinema whose meticulousness reached levels of lunacy, spends an entire movie building up a sense of wonder, mystery and awe. We're treated to the evolution of mankind from apes to tools to weapons to space travel, all set to the backdrop of perhaps the greatest cinematic score ever composed. We are given a glimpse into the future of space travel as the majestic Discovery One spacecraft slowly makes its way past Jupiter for a mysterious mission. We are introduced without much explanation to several cryptic clues involving a monolith, an otherworldly object that sparks the evolution of mankind. We are mesmerized by the trippy, psychedelic stargate sequence. Finally, the film ends with the protagonist, astronaut Dave Bowman, transformed into a cosmic fetus staring placidly at Earth.What utter, utter rubbish, I thought, after the credits rolled. I felt bamboozled, conned and downright annoyed. As I staggered out of the cinema, I remember feeling a deep sense of intellectual inadequacy. Was I too stupid to get it? Apparently not, as several other audience members were similarly confounded. The ending, as a metaphor for humanity’s next step in evolution, made no sense. The film posed far more questions than answers, which is supposed to be a good thing in art but in this occasion it came across as Kubrick being intellectually lazy. I consider my intellect to be above average and even I was struggling to grasp what Kubrick was trying to convey in the last few scenes. So what are some other of the more infamous, less celebrated but equally underwhelming endings? Cue the following.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? For me, it would have to be *Catch Me If You Can*. I’m not generally one for the 'based on a true story' genre, as I find it often morphs into some saccharine, melodramatic, and often inaccurate, retelling of events. More often than not, the filmmakers seem to prioritize sensationalism over authenticity, a frustrating habit that often leaves me feeling shortchanged. However, *Catch Me If You Can* manages to strike a near-perfect balance between factual grounding and cinematic flair, creating a compelling narrative that is both believable and entertaining. I suspect this is because they got Leonardo Di Caprio to play the central role. The film doesn’t pretend to be a documentary; it acknowledges its Hollywood sheen. Its focus is the essence of the original story, a charming scoundrel who impersonates various professions and successfully defrauds multiple entities.As a film, it’s a masterpiece. The visual aesthetics, the period-specific music, the superb characterizations all combine to create a breezy, effortlessly stylish experience reminiscent of a bygone era. What truly elevates *Catch Me If You Can*, above all the other “based on true events” flicks, is the sheer audacity of Frank Abagnale. You have to admire the sheer balls of this guy (even though what he did was wrong). To impersonate a doctor, a lawyer, a pilot, all at such a young age, and fool the world through charisma and confidence is an incredible feat. The film doesn’t shy away from the fact that Abagnale was a criminal. However, it also presents him as a sympathetic figure, driven by a troubled past and an innate desire to con his way into acceptance. The film portrays him as a sort of lovable rogue, which is why audiences are captivated by his exploits. The chase between Abagnale and the FBI agent played by Tom Hanks is a thrilling dynamic, showcasing the relentless pursuit of justice. Yet even then you are rooting for both. It's a testament to the filmmakers' skill that they can maintain this high level of tension and empathy throughout. It's an amazing film.

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? Oh boy, where to begin? As a classroom instructor, I've weathered a fair share of accusations, each one a unique blend of frustration, bewilderment, and, on occasion, amusement. There was the time a parent accused me of "favouritism" because their precious offspring, bless their heart, received a C on a particularly grueling essay. Apparently, praising another student's insightful analysis of *Hamlet* was a personal affront, a clear indication of my bias against the "less intellectually inclined". Then there was the incident with the missing stapler. A veritable crime against the sanctity of paperwork! It seemed the school’s most precious resource had vanished, and, naturally, I was the prime suspect. The implication being that a seasoned educator would stoop to pilfering stationery from the very classroom they were entrusted to guide. Honestly, the audacity! The stapler was, of course, eventually found, nestled innocently beside a particularly enthusiastic student's backpack. The case was closed, but not before a lingering shadow of suspicion. And let’s not forget the claims of "unethical grading practices." Turns out, the subtle art of assigning a "D" to a student who consistently failed to submit assignments was apparently a violation of some obscure pedagogical principle, some secret pact signed with the devil himself. These accusations, while irritating, were ultimately par for the course. They’re part and parcel of the teaching life, like rogue Sharpies and the omnipresent scent of dry-erase markers. However, the accusations that truly hit home, the ones that lingered like a persistent migraine, were those that questioned my dedication, not my competence. The insinuation that I didn't care enough, that my passion had waned, that I was merely going through the motions. Those stings cut deep, because, at the end of the day, our hearts are invested in these kids…

Why do some people not like Coldplay? After all these years, I still find it a bewilderment. Coldplay seems an innocuous band, yet their very mention can elicit a range of reactions, from mild indifference to outright derision. They’re not exactly controversial; they don't traffic in shock value or boast a particularly divisive sound. So what is it about this group that rubs so, so many the wrong way? For me, it's quite simple. Their music is a sugary concoction of the bland and the expected. They are a musical vanilla, devoid of any distinctive flavor or spice.Their lyrics are another point of contention. Often, they’re perceived as platitudinous and mawkish. They deal in platitudes about love, hope, and the beauty of the world, but they do so with such earnestness that they often come off as saccharine and, frankly, a bit embarrassing. Those who despise Coldplay often cite this sentimentality as the source of their antipathy. It’s a sentimentality that feels forced and unearned, lacking the genuine emotional depth that could redeem it.But there’s a deeper reason, I believe, that goes beyond the surface level critique of their music. Coldplay, for many, represents the quintessential corporate rock band; a perfect product manufactured for mass consumption. Their music has been widely used in commercials, TV shows, and stadium events, fostering the perception that they are more interested in appealing to the broadest possible audience than pursuing any genuine artistic vision.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? Surprisingly, I’d nominate *The Monkees* TV show. I realize it was nothing more than a televised marketing ploy, designed to sell records and merchandise to impressionable teenagers. The premise was simple, almost offensively so: a group of four young, attractive men are living together in a beach house, and they magically form a successful pop band. There was little to no plot in the beginning, and the acting often fell flat, but the show’s chaotic energy, self-aware humor, and innovative use of music and visual effects elevated it far beyond its manufactured origins. The show’s structure, especially in the first season, was pure genius, with the inclusion of short, frenetic musical numbers, slapstick humor, and fourth-wall-breaking antics, making the program feel unlike anything that came before it. The band members’ charisma was undeniable, and their musical talent, though sometimes overshadowed by the show's comedic elements, was genuine. The show took a meta approach to the idea of fame and the music industry, making it not just a show but a commentary on itself.I can't help but wonder if the show's creators, knowing that they were creating, in essence, a long-form advertisement, leaned into the absurdity of it. The result was a show that, despite its blatant commercial intentions, became a cultural touchstone, influencing countless artists and comedians. The Monkees proved that even a seemingly cynical creation could be something truly special. The show, from the music to the visual effects, was clearly made with passion and a dedication to the craft that went beyond the cynical marketing campaign it was. It was a case of art and craft colliding, creating a show that continues to entertain generations. It was a show that even a seasoned cynic like myself can’t help but smile and tap my foot to. *The Monkees* was never supposed to be as good as it was, and it is that fact that makes it so damn noteworthy.

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? It's quite a fascinating subject, this notion of an actor inhabiting a villainous persona so utterly, so convincingly, that it leaves an unsettling residue long after the credits roll. For me, the gold standard in that realm has always been Anthony Hopkins and his portrayal of Hannibal Lecter. It wasn't just the chillingly calm voice, the predatory stillness in his eyes, or the sardonic wit that dripped with malice; it was the complete and utter absence of anything even remotely human. He was a smooth sociopath, an intellectual predator, a shark in a bespoke suit. The way he toyed with Clarice Starling, the almost playful way he dissected his victims both literally and figuratively, was utterly mesmerizing and yet horrifying. I remember watching *The Silence of the Lambs* for the first time as a teenager, and the effect was profound. I had this strange sensation that Lecter was watching me through the screen.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? Oh, where to begin? The sheer volume of vapid pronouncements that cascade from the mouths of humanity is enough to induce a perpetual state of eye-rolling. First and foremost, there's the parade of “inspirational” quotes, those saccharine nuggets of wisdom plastered across social media, usually accompanied by a blurry sunset or a motivational picture of an alpaca. "Live, laugh, love." "Be the change you wish to see in the world." Give over! These platitudes, repeated ad nauseam, feel less like genuine profundity and more like carefully constructed distractions from the crushing banality of existence. Then there are the unsolicited life coaches, the self-proclaimed gurus dispensing advice they clearly haven’t even bothered to apply to their own lives. "You just need to believe in yourself!" they’ll declare, as if self-doubt is just some fleeting inconvenience, easily banished with a positive affirmation and a kale smoothie. I’m not against self-improvement, by any means. But these people are often all show and no substance. The most eye-roll-inducing, however, are the declarations of unwavering expertise from those who have absolutely no clue what they're talking about. The ones who, armed with a cursory Google search, feel qualified to debate anything and everything, from quantum physics to the complexities of international law. These are the know-it-alls, the ones who see shades of grey only in the rearview mirror, and pronounce their half-baked opinions as absolute truths. I find myself increasingly unable to resist the urge to interject with the most condescending of sneers, just so that they have to confront the ridiculousness of their own pronouncements.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? Years ago I worked as a lowly clerk in a corporate office. A job so monotonous and mundane that the monotony was almost meditative. In a windowless basement, the only sunlight came from the flickering fluorescent tubes above. My main, solitary task was to compile, collate and staple documents for distribution throughout the building. In this job I was a cog in a well oiled, soulless machine, an insignificant pawn in a game of chess. My boss was a quiet, timid man who was so nice one felt sorry for him. His immediate superior was the quintessential corporate jerk. A short, stocky man with beady eyes and a permanent scowl ingrained on his face, as though every single moment of his life brought immeasurable distress. He was the kind that would wear one of those annoying 'world's best boss' mugs to work. One such day the head of the department came down to peruse our department and asked us to rate our current workload on a scale of 1-10. Being the most junior, I was called upon to explain and without thinking, I blurted out that I thought the workload was a 2. The reason I replied in such fashion was because I had a genuine desire to tell them. I did not have a whole lot of work to do. I loved my job, I would have been happy doing it the rest of my life. I arrived early, always stayed and I spent my time learning the inner workings of the office. The next day, I was hauled up to my boss’ office. My boss, looking pale, informed me that I was being accused of insubordination and laziness by one of my colleagues. This colleague, I soon found out, was the office social butterfly. A woman whose sole existence was to gossip, ingratiate herself with all those above with the hope of getting ahead and back stabbing those below. The actual reason for the accusation of insubordination was that I had called the workload a 2. The accusation of laziness was that the workload was a 2. In other words, according to this woman, I was ‘trying to make her look bad’ by claiming the workload was easy. My boss, a nervous and mild-mannered man, did not want to become embroiled in an argument. Thus, he took the word of the gossip and told me that I should probably consider my future in the company. The corporate jerk was also present in the meeting. He sneered at me, the type of sneer that was more common among bad guys in a Bond movie or the ones you might see in a high school bully. I was bewildered. How had I, in a company of hundreds of employees, managed to become a target by simply answering a question? The most ridiculous part was that the workload WAS easy. But of course the gossip wanted to look good and be seen working hard to earn her paycheck. I then realized that in such environments, hard work really doesn’t pay, pretending to work hard pays. I was eventually let go from that job and I had to face the harrowing unemployment market where I was forced to take on many demeaning jobs. I learnt a valuable lesson that day: In the corporate world, there are always backstabbers and you must always remember to watch your back.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? The truth is, I wasn’t particularly astute at recognising red flags in my younger days. In fact, I was more accustomed to wearing rose-tinted glasses, especially when the prospect of a better future was dangling temptingly before me. However, if I were to cast my mind back to those halcyon days of youthful ambition and recall a situation preceding an employment offer where I should've sounded the alarm, it would unequivocally be my first proper job - not the warehouse stint with Vanessa Milan, but a position at a prominent tech firm. I was young and fresh out of university, brimming with idealism and the conviction that I, too, could conquer the world of Silicon Valley. The interview process was an exercise in flattery. I was wined and dined, my every achievement lauded, and my potential meticulously cataloged. The team seemed brilliant, the work stimulating, and the perks, like an in-house masseuse and catered lunches, were simply the icing on the cake. The offer came, generous and promising, and I, blinded by the prospect of career advancement and fast money, accepted it without a second thought. Yet, in retrospect, there were tell-tale signs, tiny tremors that I now recognise as the foundations of a crumbling edifice. First, the hiring manager, a man whose handshake could crush a watermelon, spent a considerable amount of time discussing his own financial success, going on and on about luxury cars and offshore accounts. Secondly, although the team seemed brilliant on the surface and I would have sworn blind how innovative and groundbreaking they were on their presentations, there was an undercurrent of competitiveness, an atmosphere of each man for himself and every deal. The meetings devolved into passive-aggressive power plays, each team member trying to outsmart the other. Finally, the company, in its desperation to get me to sign, kept pushing the idea of a "team-building" weekend retreat, a thinly veiled attempt to get us all together in a remote location to "bond." I declined, and their tone noticeably shifted. My gut instinct then, as it often does, was spot on warning me to stay far away, yet I ignored it as I have often ignored several important things in my life. I ended up working there for a year, a year filled with endless meetings, backstabbing colleagues, and an increasingly demanding work environment. The in-house masseuse was the only perk worth mentioning. In the end, I packed my bags and left, battered and bruised. If only I had heeded the warning signals before signing on the dotted line. If only I had done my due diligence. If only I had listened to my gut. Perhaps, then, I would have dodged a bullet and saved myself a year of unnecessary misery.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? I'm not a big fan of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. You would think that me saying that would be akin to me proclaiming that I was not a fan of breathing air, as the constant barrage of praise and cultural saturation of those films would suggest. To be honest, I understand the appeal. The films are generally competently made, the acting ranges from pretty good to Oscar-worthy in some instances, and the special effects would make Georges Méliès soil himself with envy. Moreover, the narrative usually ties everything up in a neat little bow by the end credits, which is ideal for the average moviegoer. But I just find them profoundly…. boring. And formulaic. And overrated. And at this point, a bit exhausting. They've become the cinematic equivalent of fast food; readily available, easy to digest, and ultimately unsatisfying. Each installment feels like a cog in a pre-ordained machine, churning out the same beats, the same quips, the same predictable outcomes. There’s a lack of genuine risk, a fear of deviating from the established playbook, and a relentless focus on expanding the franchise rather than telling compelling – or even remotely novel – stories.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? That would be easy. I’d have selected that one photo, the only one that captured the essence of complete and utter despair. A photo taken the day after the incident. The incident I loathe even mentioning, let alone dwelling upon. The picture was taken on a bright, unforgivingly sunny day, the kind that usually imbues a sense of vitality and hope. This time around, the sun only served to highlight the utter desolation of the scene. The photo portrays a simple, unadorned courtyard. A banal, grey concrete square enclosed by a low brick wall. Beyond the wall there was nothing, save for an unkempt meadow and a few spindly, half-dead trees, which only seemed to amplify the bleakness. In the center of the courtyard, slightly off-kilter, was a solitary, metal bench, painted a faded, peeling blue. The seat, in its current state, offered no comfort. The paint was chipped and flaked off, revealing patches of rust, and the metal struts appeared twisted and strained under the weight of some indiscernible force. In the background of the picture there were a few other people going about their routines, with one sitting at a picnic table, as if nothing had happened. Then, right in the foreground. Me. Sitting on the bench, head slumped, shoulders hunched. I was wearing a grey t-shirt, the colour of the sky before a storm. What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? One of the most pervasive errors I've observed in nascent parents is the relentless pursuit of perfection. They strive to present a flawless façade, projecting an image of effortless competence that, frankly, none of us can truly attain. It's as if they've forgotten they're navigating uncharted waters, stumbling and falling like any novice. This is particularly noticeable when these parents begin comparing themselves to others, especially the seemingly polished families they observe on social media. They become consumed by meticulously curated feeds, showcasing idyllic lives, and inadvertently cultivate an internal pressure that is frankly, counterproductive. The relentless emphasis on perfection leaves them vulnerable to crippling self-doubt, preventing them from enjoying the journey of child-rearing and, conversely, inhibiting their children from experiencing the genuine and accepting love that creates a secure foundation. Instead of embracing the inevitable imperfections of family life, these parents often overcompensate. They become hyper-critical, not only of themselves, but also of their children, and create an environment rife with anxiety and unrealistic expectations.So how do they rectify such glaring foibles? First, they must cultivate self-compassion. They need to acknowledge that they are human, prone to making mistakes, and it is perfectly acceptable. Let go of the notion that they must always have all the answers, and be willing to seek guidance from trusted sources, whether from experienced friends, relatives, or professionals. Second, be present. Put down the phone more and focus on the child. Engage with their world, even if the world is a messy pile of toys or crayon-drawn faces. These are the things that create intimacy and memories, and the truly valuable outcomes in a child's journey. Third, and perhaps most crucially, embrace the reality of imperfection. Encourage a home in which vulnerability is acknowledged, where mistakes may be spoken of openly and often, instead of concealed and stigmatized. The goal is to raise a happy, resilient child, not an image of flawless perfection that may never exist. By focusing on connection, understanding, and acceptance, parents can cultivate a healthy environment where children can thrive, where their character is ultimately forged in the fires of mistakes as opposed to the sterile perfection of a false world that cannot be maintained.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? It’s a question that hangs heavy in the air, a specter that haunts any conversation about the two continents. To paint either Europe or the USA with a broad brush of racism, I feel, would be a gross oversimplification, a disservice to the complex tapestry of history, social dynamics, and individual experiences that shape our understanding of prejudice. Both regions grapple with a legacy of discrimination, born of conquest, colonization, and the insidious creep of ideology that values one group over another. I have lived in both regions and it is very difficult for me to say which country is more racist. It depends.The sad truth is that if you want to find racism, you don’t need to go far. The USA's history is plastered - in very large writing - across the pages of your history books. The enslavement of Africans, the Jim Crow South, the relentless persecution of Native Americans – these are scars that continue, in some ways, to fester. Yet, the USA also boasts a vibrant civil rights movement, an ongoing struggle for equality that, while far from perfect, has achieved remarkable progress in dismantling legal segregation and fighting for equal rights. There is no such thing as a utopia, a place where every single person lives in peace with each other. The USA still has a long way to go.The same goes for Europe. European history includes the Holocaust perpetrated by the Nazis, and the systematic elimination of Roma people, not to forget the rampant xenophobia that has reared its unwelcome head during times of economic and societal hardship. In my past experiences I have seen European countries openly discuss having as little immigration from certain countries as possible. As a Trinidadian with very dark skin, on my travels, I have been shocked at the amount of times I have been stared at in Europe. I have felt this to a larger degree in certain European countries as opposed to the USA and it has left me feeling slightly intimidated at times. Whether these stares are born of genuine curiosity, cultural gaps, or outright bigotry is difficult to pinpoint, but the weight of such attention can be undeniable. Whether America's current problems with race are substantially worse than Europe is very difficult to say.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? Without a shadow of a doubt, the most underestimated villain in the horror movie pantheon has to be the insidious, ever-present entity that lurks within the walls of a seemingly idyllic suburban home: the poltergeist. We are not talking about your run-of-the-mill, run-for-your-life boogeyman brand of monster; no, this villain is far more cunning, subtle, and ultimately, terrifyingly realistic. The poltergeist’s power doesn’t lie in brute force or grotesque appearance. Instead, its reign of terror functions in the manipulation of environment, the warping of perceptions, and the insidious corrosion of sanity. Often, it’s not a creature you can readily see or fight; it’s an invisible puppeteer, pulling the strings of domesticity until the once-stable fabric of a family unravels thread by agonizing thread. Consider the traditional horror film tropes that the poltergeist transcends. The slasher flicks, the chainsaw massacres--all serve up a certain level of visceral, easy-to-digest fear. You *see* the danger, you *understand* the threat. But the poltergeist? It's a slow-burn, a symphony of dread that creeps into your bones, often starting with the mundane: a flickering light, a misplaced object, an inexplicably chilling draft. These seemingly innocuous occurrences are then carefully layered into a masterfully crafted crescendo of paranoia and despair.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? I had a difficult time in my pre-teen years, marked by a lot of turmoil and strife in my family. I was a timid, introspective lad; easily intimidated and often lost in my own thoughts. This made me an easy target for the bullies in my class. Their routine was relentless, every day the same: taunts, shoves, having my books and lunch thrown on the ground; it was a never-ending cycle of misery. I didn’t tell anyone, I was too ashamed. My parents were already dealing with enough problems, so I bottled everything up, suffering in silence. One particular day, it was especially bad. They had cornered me behind the school, ripped up my homework, and were about to start on my brand new shoes. Just as they were about to inflict further humiliation, out of nowhere came Mr. Davidson, the kindly old janitor. He was a man of few words, but a heart of gold. He saw everything. He didn’t say anything to the bullies, but shooed them away with a stern look. Then, rather than the usual reprimand, he knelt and quietly helped me gather my scattered belongings; he picked up my tattered homework and wiped away the dirt from my shoes and clothes with a wet rag. He didn't offer platitudes, just a gentle, knowing silence. That moment of unexpected compassion from a man who understood the subtle nuances of childhood cruelty remains etched in my memory. He didn't need to speak; his actions conveyed far more than any words could. He didn't seek recognition, and he didn't make a fuss. He simply did what was right. Seeing my dishevelled condition, he took me into the janitor’s closet, and gave me a new pair of shoes he happened to have for a few students. As he did so, he offered me a sandwich. I felt so much warmth despite the terrible events earlier. He was a quiet hero, who, in that small act of kindness and generosity, restored my faith in humanity and turned the tide on years of relentless bullying. I never forgot his kindness.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? The truth of the matter is, I often feel like I'm a walking contradiction. When pressed on the specifics of my daily grind, a flush of embarrassment invariably creeps up my neck. “What do you *do*?”, they'll ask, their eyes alight with a curiosity I can only meet with a vague, evasive smile. To utter the words, "I'm a custodian," feels like a confession of failure. A declaration that I’ve somehow fallen short of expectations, of the societal ladder of prestige. But what is the best way to avoid the dreaded “C” word, without outright lying or sounding like a deluded fool? I've mulled over this conundrum countless times, searching for that perfect, palatable phrase. I’ve considered the more elaborate options - "sanitation engineer," perhaps, or "environmental maintenance specialist" - but they always sound forced, like I'm trying too hard to impress. Or perhaps taking an honest approach, and saying “I maintain the upkeep of a school.” After all, whether I’m mopping floors or emptying bins, I’m doing work, and for all my efforts, I think it would be a nice gesture of respect to myself, and for others to treat me with the same.

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? I have always wondered about that question. The Olympics are a magnificent spectacle, a testament to human endeavor, skill, and the unrelenting pursuit of excellence. Yet, amidst all the glorious displays of athleticism and sportsmanship, there's a peculiar phenomenon: why is the bronze medal winner often visibly happier than the silver medalist? The answer, it seems, lies in the realm of cognitive psychology, specifically, counterfactual thinking.Counterfactual thinking, simply put, is the act of mentally simulating "what ifs." It's the human tendency to construct alternative scenarios, to imagine how things could have been different. And here's where the medal stand reveals its psychological paradox. For the silver medalist, the "what if" scenario is brutally clear: "What if I had performed just a tiny bit better? What if I had exerted just a little more effort? I could have won gold!" This proximity to the gold medal, the almost-achievement, can trigger feelings of disappointment, regret, and a potent sense of having fallen short of their ultimate goal. The alternative reality – the one where victory was within reach – looms large, casting a shadow over the achievement.

What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? It was a balmy Tuesday; the sun's rays, a warm embrace, as I strolled through the bustling marketplace, a hive of activity and bartering. Vendors hollered out their wares, the air thick with the aroma of spices, the chatter of haggling customers, and the clatter of coins. I, a curious observer in this theater of commerce, found myself drawn to a stall overflowing with vibrant, counterfeit designer watches – Rolexes, Omegas, all flaunting a deceptive sheen. It’s a common scam, I thought, but this particular charade was the most minuscule I had ever witnessed, both in scale and audacity. Perched precariously on a flimsy stool sat a man, his face creased with what could pass for genuine concern, or maybe just a lack of sleep. He beckoned me over, flashing a dazzling smile, and began his pitch, which sounded scripted and rehearsed, no doubt he used multiple times a day. "My friend, I assure you these are, how you say, the real deal. Swiss-made! You can compare to any watch shop in city! Very high quality!" He then proceeded to offer them at a price that made my eyebrows arch in disbelief. He was practically giving them away! "A special price, only for you!" he insisted, patting my shoulder with a familiarity I hadn't earned. A subtle glance at the other customers revealed knowing smirks, a collective understanding that I, the unsuspecting tourist, was his next target. I feigned interest, examining a particularly egregious Rolex replica. The date window was crooked, the hands wobbling, and the second hand ticked with a blatant disregard for precision. It was a comical attempt at deception, a blatant knockoff that even a novice could spot. The man, sensing my hesitation, leaned in conspiratorially. "Look!" he declared, pulling out a magnifying glass, "See the detail! Magnificent!" He proceeded to run the glass over the watch, showing, to absolutely nobody's surprise, that the watch was actually worse up close. He then gestured to a discreet box hidden beneath the stall, hinting at secret caches of "genuine" merchandise. I, in a playful spirit, decided to engage in his theatrical display. "Tell you what," I said, with a slight smile, "I'll take that gold one… if you throw in that magnifying glass." The man’s face fell. His wide smile evaporated, replaced by a look of bewildered annoyance. The bravado vanished. He simply grunted, turned, and started to put all the watches back in their boxes. The scam, it seemed, was over. No dramatic denouement, no drawn-out argument, just a swift concession to the futility of his enterprise. It was, in every sense, a miniature swindle, a petty deception that amounted to nothing more than, perhaps, a slight dent in the pride of a very bad salesman. The sheer insignificance of the operation made it amusing. I gave him a sympathetic nod and moved on, leaving him to his reflections, and his now-useless magnifying glass.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? When I think of a Hollywood movie that is far removed from any possible spectrum of realism, this movie always comes to my mind. You can tell by just watching the poster that this is going to be another formulaic family movie; the white background which signifies that this movie will have no content, dialogue or subplot other than this generic couple and their darned dog, the smiling figures staring at you almost sinisterly, the tepid humour of a puppy leading the couple by leash. “A dog leading its masters by leash?…….. that's so clever and ironic!” Sarcasms and cynicisms aside, here are the reasons why this movie is not just a wrong depiction of US life but an offense to ordinary people who tighten their belt and blue collar while slaving it on the 9 to 5. 1. Raising a dog = good practice for raising children, according to this movie. The above image perfectly captures how stupid that notion is. No one would watch a photo like this and and say that this is evidence of good parental skills. Besides feeding and caring there is nothing remotely similar to raising dogs as compared to children. This is a notion you tend to see solely in Hollywood movies where raising children can be condescended to the same level as keeping a litter of puppies. Raising good children, especially for poorer parents, is practically a lifelong sacrifice and the ultimate moral contract. Giving up your youth, freedom and finances and being willing to shield your child from incoming physical harm or even death is not the same as a bowl of Kibbles n Bits and a scratch on the tummy. 2. Every middle class American lives in a mansion on a sprawling well-kept spread of land. Owen Wilson and Jennifer Aniston's characters are ordinary reporters with two kids. She becomes a stay at home mom which makes him the breadwinner. His highest paying position is at The Philadelphia Inquirer which, according to online research, currently has an average annual salary of $60,000. This would mean that his monthly salary would've been around $5000 give or take. This 16 acre five bedroom Pennsylvania farmhouse had a selling price of $1.25 million in 2011. Using a mortgage calculator based on local interest rates at the time his payment for the house would’ve been roughly $5800 per month based on a 30 year loan repayment. So in other words, for the family to have realistically lived such a lifestyle, Jennifer Aniston's character had to have employed some means of soliciting tax-free money at night. 3. Let's all shed tears……. A dog has died of old age. This was the moment that was the straw that broke the camel's back. We ejected the DVD in sheer annoyance and frustration at this point. The dog died……a natural death. Cue sad music and flashbacks. How entitled can your country be if the natural death of a dog can elicit tears from an audience? A pet dog in Trinidad is lucky to live past 8 years, even in the best of care. My own backyard where I grew up contains the remains of over a dozen unfortunate cats and canines who died prematurely due to illness, speeding cars and just plain bad luck. We had not a single pet that died of natural causes i.e. old age. If we did, we would have celebrated its life and the fact that it led a full life. This supposed tearjerking scene was just another alienating Hollywoodism that highlights how out of touch the film industry is. What an awful movie full of delusional perceptions of the average American life. Don't watch it.4. The single parent, struggling with two minimum wadge earning jobs while living in a tenement gets to share a heartfelt moment with his children…… in a brand new, spacious, modern house, with a new car parked in the drive way. This is another trope often seen in Hollywood movies and quite frankly it's insulting to those who have to work multiple shifts to cater for the most basic of needs. A few years ago my cousin, a qualified but unemployed carpenter went to New York on a vacation and got a job as a waiter. He hated it and it was exhausting and paid poor wages. However the movies try to portray that sort of job as like a stepping stone to riches and endless possibilities. In reality you could be serving meals wearing a ridiculous plastic smile while dreaming and thinking that your life is going to be like that of the characters on screen. Even if your job gets you any sort of promotion your life would never be like this. The movie also conveniently portrays the waiter having time to cultivate relationships with other equally struggling individuals and make bold decisions about his life. The truth is as a waiter you don’t have the time, the energy or the money to make changes to your situation. You’re working on a treadmill trying to survive, doing all that you are capable of just to have a roof over your head and to eat.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? There is a movie that still resonates with me to this day, a film that transported me from the confines of my worn-out couch to the heart of its tumultuous narrative. It was a low-budget indie film, bereft of any A-list actors or extravagant special effects, yet it remains forever etched in my memory. It was gritty, raw, and unapologetically real, and the realism was so pronounced that I felt as if I was an invisible observer, privy to the characters' most intimate moments. I could practically smell the stale cigarettes and cheap beer that permeated the dimly lit bar where the film's protagonists spent a considerable amount of time. Every creak of the floorboards, every hushed conversation, every fleeting expression of anguish or joy – it all felt palpably authentic, as if I were breathing the same air as the characters. The movie in question was shot almost entirely on location, which added a certain distinct aura to its authenticity. This choice of filming location coupled with the lack of professional actors added to the realistic nature of the movie. The characters were flawed, their decisions often questionable, and their lives messy, much like the real people I’d encountered in my own life.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? I often find myself pondering this question, particularly when staring at the golden arches, the siren song of a drive-thru, or the tantalizing images on a menu board. Let's face it: fast food, in its relentless pursuit of profit, can employ some rather underhanded strategies to separate you from your hard-earned cash. One of the most pervasive tactics, a true art form, is the manipulation of portion sizes. They're masters of the subtle shift. A few less fries in your container. A slightly smaller soda cup. These incremental reductions, imperceptible to the casual observer, add up to significant savings for these corporate behemoths. The aim? To trick us into craving more, forcing us to order additional items and driving up the average check. And let's not forget the "value meals." They're often a carefully constructed illusion of a bargain. You might think you're getting a deal by bundling a burger, fries, and a drink together. Yet, when you break things down, you realize that you might be paying more than if you’d ordered each item a la carte. It's a clever psychological maneuver, making us feel that we're getting a discount, when, in reality, we’re being subtly upsold. This is especially true when new, eye-catching items are added to the so called value meal. Another dirty trick involves the strategic placement of items on the menu. The expensive, high-profit items, the ones they really want to sell, often sit front and center. Eye-catching photos, and large, bold fonts are used to grab attention. The cheaper, often healthier options, are relegated to the margins, or even hidden. It is all about manipulation of what the customer focuses on.

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? This is a tricky situation, one that needs to be handled with a delicate touch and a dash of pragmatism. The knee-jerk reaction, of course, is to consider them a killjoy, a grump, an ungrateful employee who doesn't appreciate the perks of the job. However, a more nuanced approach is required. Before I start throwing the book at them, I would need to understand the "why" behind their aversion. Is it a genuine dislike of forced social interactions? Perhaps they are introverted, or simply find the whole thing excruciatingly boring. Or maybe there is a more valid reason. Are they uncomfortable with the boisterous atmosphere? Do they have childcare issues that prevent them from staying late? Is there an underlying conflict with a colleague or a deeply rooted personal conviction? Whatever the cause, a dialogue is paramount. Assuming they are a good employee, the first step would be a private conversation. The aim isn't to force them to attend, but to understand their perspective. I'd begin by listening more than talking, offering a safe space for them to voice their concerns. If their reason for not wanting to attend is merely a personal preference, I'd be inclined to let it slide, provided their work performance and team interactions aren’t negatively impacted. You cannot force someone to enjoy themselves. However, if their refusal is rooted in a deeper issue, such as a workplace conflict or a feeling of exclusion, then that warrants the attention of upper management. In such cases, the priority shifts to resolving the underlying problem. Ultimately, I am not going to be the hardline boss who insists that all employees attend company parties, the thought process that does nothing but cause resentment and alienation within a team. A good, sensible manager understands that a happy employee equals a productive employee, and trying to force them to socialize— if it doesn't make them happy— is counterproductive.

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? Sometimes, what gnaws at me isn't a grand injustice or a societal ill, but something utterly trivial, something that most people probably wouldn't give a second thought. It's those seemingly innocuous things that burrow under my skin and fester into a low-grade, simmering irritation. Top of the list? People who don't know how to use a public drinking fountain. You know the ones: They jam the nozzle into their mouths, creating a germ-ridden environment for the next user. Or they let the water gush out aimlessly, drenching the floor and wasting precious drops. This wasn't always a problem, mind you. Growing up, I didn’t ponder the proper etiquette of accessing a potable water source. But a series of events transformed this into a full-blown pet peeve. A string of trips around the world and an excessive amount of trips to the gym and I was constantly using public fountains.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? There are quite a few cinematic abject failures that have incited visceral reactions within me over the years, ranging from mild annoyance to incandescent rage. One such picture comes to mind immediately. It started off promisingly enough with a fairly compelling premise: a seasoned astronaut makes a perilous solo journey across the galaxy to a distant planet in search of habitable life forms. The first forty minutes, filled with breathtaking visuals and an immersive soundscape, held my attention. The astronaut, a grizzled type, was portrayed by a seasoned actor with an uncanny ability to express volumes with just his eyes, and the audience was hooked. Suddenly, the film lurched violently off course. After encountering a seemingly benign alien species, the narrative descended into an endless litany of nonsensical philosophy and pseudo-intellectual drivel. Characters started spouting incomprehensible jargon about the nature of existence and the futility of human endeavor. The beautiful cinematography and rich musical score became an irritating backdrop to the mind-numbing dialogue. The script, if one could even call it that, seemed to have been written by a teenager who'd stumbled upon a philosophy textbook and, believing themselves to be the second coming of Sartre, felt compelled to impart their newfound wisdom on the world. I found myself growing increasingly agitated, my brow furrowed in a mixture of confusion and annoyance. Every attempt to make sense of the plot was met with another convoluted pronouncement. The breaking point came when the astronaut, after spending the last hour pontificating with a sentient rock formation, decided to convert to a religion, alien in origin and inexplicable even to the supposed faithful. I stood up from my seat, a wave of disgusted exasperation washing over me and I left the auditorium. I didn't even bother to see the end. The experience left me with nothing but a sour taste in my mouth and a deep-seated resentment towards the film’s writer and director. I was left with a feeling of having had my time and money ruthlessly stolen from me.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? One glaring inconsistency that has always irked me is the ending of the film ‘Inception.’ It’s a film that I, for the most part, admire for its ingenuity and ambition in constructing this multi-layered dream world. The intricate details woven throughout the narrative, the mind-bending visuals, the philosophical ponderings on reality – all of it is undeniably captivating. But that ending… the spinning top. The lack of a definitive answer to whether Cobb (DiCaprio) is still in a dream or finally back in the real world is the very definition of a narrative conundrum. We see him reunite with his children, a moment charged with such powerful emotion that we, the audience, are equally invested in its authenticity. He doesn’t seem to care about the top spinning, he’s home. Does that denote it’s all real? Then why does the top wobble unnaturally? The uncertainty is, perhaps, the point. It’s supposed to leave us pondering the nature of reality. But it’s also a cop-out, a somewhat lazy way to conclude a movie that is otherwise so meticulous and thoughtfully constructed. For me, that final, ambiguous shot feels incomplete, like the filmmakers either chickened out of providing a concrete resolution or, even worse, lost the plot somewhere along the way, perhaps in its own dream state.

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? When assessing the landscape of Hollywood's fading stars, a certain melancholic air descends, akin to witnessing the slow, inexorable bloom and subsequent withering of a radiant, exotic flower. I often wonder what happened to Freddie Prinze Jr.? The man oozed charisma, charm and had a face you could bet your life on, yet aside from his marriage to Sarah Michelle Gellar (which is its own kind of success), he never really ascended to the A-list. Perhaps the industry, in its capricious nature, deemed him a one-hit wonder, forever typecast by his roles. Another name that invariably springs to mind is Josh Hartnett. He, too, possessed that quintessential Hollywood package – the brooding good looks, the undeniable screen presence. He was practically a shoo-in for stardom. Then, poof! He morphed into a supporting actor, taking roles that didn't really showcase the star potential that he had. I have heard rumors that his reluctance to get into the whole celebrity status bubble, the incessant red-carpet events, may be the reason for his career not progressing to the heights it should have. This reluctance, however, seemed to have cost him dearly. There's also Brendan Fraser, a man who, in the annals of Hollywood, deserves a second act. He had the It factor, the humor, the physicality, the perfect blend of action and comedy. He was literally everywhere in the late 1990s and early 2000s, but a combination of health issues, the sheer unreliability of the industry, and maybe some bad roles, saw his trajectory decline. It goes to show you that Hollywood is an unforgiving beast, constantly hungry for new faces and new stories, and it can easily dismiss even those who seem destined for immortality in the blink of an eye.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? I’ve always wondered, what is the secret etiquette understood amongst fast-food workers and those who frequent their establishments? I am not talking about the usual ‘thank you’ and ‘you’re welcome’ pleasantries but rather the underlying, unspoken rules that dictate their interactions. I would venture to say I am a familiar face at numerous fast-food joints, a fact that has occurred to me with some reflection. Take, for instance, the drive-thru attendant, always with the same cursory greeting, a practiced smile masking their true sentiments. Are they judging my order? Do they remember my penchant for extra ketchup, or the fact that I invariably order a large soda, even if I’m only getting a burger? It’s a peculiar relationship, this brief dance of commerce, and I can’t help but believe that a hierarchy exists, unspoken, unwritten, and yet deeply understood. Is there a specific status given to the regulars? The ones who walk in daily, perhaps even multiple times? Do they get preferential treatment, a larger portion of fries, an extra packet of sauce? Or are they viewed with a mixture of pity and disdain? Maybe they become a sort of running joke, a source of amusement for those trapped in the monotony of their jobs. "Ah, here comes John again, ordering his usual heart attack," one might quip. Or, more darkly, "He's back. He's never going to learn." Perhaps they envy us, the freedom we have to choose where we eat, or perhaps they simply look upon us with a detached, professional courtesy, dealing with each customer, daily. Regardless, the unspoken rules of the fast-food transaction, the invisible contracts, the quiet judgments, intrigue me. I often catch myself wondering what would happen if I didn’t say, ‘Thank you’ and simply drove off. Would I get away with it? Or would I be forever labeled, a scofflaw of the Golden Arches, condemned to eternal shame?

What is legal but ethically wrong? I've always been fascinated by the labyrinthine relationship between legality and morality, how something can be perfectly within the bounds of the law yet still manage to leave a bitter taste in one's mouth, a sense of unease, a feeling of being somehow… wrong. It's a philosophical quandary that often surfaces in the most unexpected corners of life, a reminder that just because we *can* do something doesn't necessarily mean we *should*. Take, for instance, the relentless pursuit of profit by pharmaceutical companies. They develop life-saving drugs, there's no denying that, and it's all perfectly legal. But the price gouging, the exorbitant markups that render these essential medicines inaccessible to the very people who need them most– that’s where ethics gets trampled. The CEOs of these companies continue to line their pockets with vast fortunes, all while the less fortunate are left to wither away.Consider also the ubiquitous practice of lobbying. Politicians, the very people entrusted to shape our laws, are routinely courted by special interest groups, the giants of industry. These groups shower them with incentives, funding their campaigns, underwriting their lavish lifestyles. All perfectly legal, all above board. Yet, the result is often a perversion of the democratic process, a system rigged to favor the wealthy and well-connected, at the expense of the common good. The scales tip, the balance is lost. What had integrity is now corrupted by greed. Or, one could delve into the murky world of offshore tax shelters. Corporations and wealthy individuals, in the name of financial efficiency, stash their assets in tax havens, avoiding their civic duty to contribute to the infrastructure and public services that underpin society. It's all sanctioned by the law, enabled even, but the ethical implications are staggering. It leaves us all in the lurch. It is a system built on pilfering and greed. It’s a drain on resources that could otherwise be used for schools, hospitals, and social programs. It is a silent crime, a legal loophole that perpetuates inequality, leaving the majority to bear the burdens of a system warped by self-interest. These are just a few examples, but they all illustrate the same crucial point: The law is not an infallible arbiter of right and wrong. It is written by humans, interpreted by humans, and influenced by the same biases, prejudices, and self-serving interests that plague us all. The pursuit of profit, the hunger for power, the temptation of wealth… These are the forces that often blur the lines between what is legal and what is morally defensible. And it's in that grey area, that moral twilight, that we find some of the most pressing ethical challenges of our time.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? I’d have to opt for Alejandro Jodorowsky’s *Holy Mountain*. When I first saw it, I was utterly gobsmacked. The visuals are so bizarre, so hallucinatory, so utterly unpredictable, that you’re never quite sure what you’re looking at. One minute you're gazing upon a bizarre procession of people in elaborate, esoteric costumes climbing an enormous tower, the next you're witnessing a frog being transformed into a majestic horse, or the alchemical transformation of swords into flowers. The film is a visual feast, a riot of color and imagery that assaults the senses. It's a film that challenges your preconceptions, a film that demands your attention and refuses to be ignored. However, the thing about *Holy Mountain* is that it’s far more than just eye candy, it’s a cinematic experience that's hard to quantify, its meaning elusive, its impact profound. What makes it worth watching is that it's unlike anything else you'll ever see. I wouldn't say it's an easy film to enjoy, but it's unquestionably a rewarding one if you stick with it. The narrative is abstract and allegorical, but there are recurring themes of spiritual awakening, occultism, and the destructive nature of materialism. The characters are archetypal and symbolic; the Thief, the Alchemist, the Ego. Jodorowsky, as a director, throws everything he has at the screen. He constructs elaborate sets, utilises outlandish costumes and makeup, fills the frame with an abundance of visual detail. The experience is overwhelming, intoxicating, and occasionally, deeply unsettling. It's a bizarre and often bewildering voyage through the spiritual and psychological landscape. But it is a voyage nonetheless. The film stays with you long after the credits roll, a reminder of the power of cinema to challenge and provoke. I’ve watched this movie countless times. It continues to fascinate me, to make me question the world around me. And that, I think, is the mark of a truly great film.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? It's a tough call, choosing just one. Over the years, a plethora of characters have etched themselves in my memory. But if I had to choose, it would be someone shrouded in the mist of ambiguity, a figure who operates in the shadows, a master of deception and misdirection. I’m thinking of a character with a keen intellect, dry wit, and an almost supernatural ability to navigate the treacherous waters of human folly. A character who, despite their flaws, remains stubbornly human. This individual, though fictional, feels more real than many I've encountered in the flesh. They are a constant reminder that the world isn't black and white, that morality is a sliding scale, and that even the most complex individuals are, at their core, just trying to survive. Their actions, though sometimes questionable, are always driven by a sense of purpose, a desire to either dismantle corruption or uphold a fragile sense of order, depending on your viewpoint. They are, in essence, a reflection of ourselves, our struggles, our doubts and our desperate need for resolution in an otherwise chaotic reality. Someone who reminds us that we are all flawed, all capable of both great good and terrible evil, and that the line between the two is often blurred. It is this very ambiguity, this refusal to be easily categorized, that makes them such a fascinating and enduring presence in my literary life.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? It's a rather fascinating question, and one that, considering the evolution of the film industry, is riddled with complexities. My initial inclination leans towards a resounding 'yes,' but then again, the Hollywood landscape of yesteryear was a vastly different beast. Brad Pitt undoubtedly possesses the quintessential leading-man physique - the chiseled jawline, the piercing blue eyes, the physique sculpted to perfection. These were, and still are, essential ingredients for Hollywood stardom, regardless of era. He oozes a certain effortless charisma, a blend of cool confidence and boyish charm that is undeniably appealing. Think of the effortless way he steals scenes in *Ocean's Eleven,* or the vulnerability he somehow conveys in *Fight Club*.However, classic Hollywood prized a level of polish and theatricality that Pitt, in his more understated performances, doesn't always exhibit. The likes of Cary Grant, Humphrey Bogart, and Clark Gable were masters of the pronouncements, the grand gestures, the perfectly timed facial expressions that could fill a theater. There was an undeniable emphasis on diction, on projecting both voice and presence. Pitt’s more modern approach, a naturalistic style that leans towards subtle nuance, might have been considered almost a little too *understated* for the silver screen of the 1930s and 40s.Furthermore, the studio system, the lifeblood of classic Hollywood, was a ruthless machine, churning out stars and demanding unwavering loyalty. Could Pitt have navigated the strict contracts, the constant scrutiny, the carefully curated image that defined the careers back then? He’s proven himself a savvy businessman, a producer of note. Yet, navigating the power plays and the demanding roles, the gossip and the constant media attention, may very well have been a daunting feat to the Pitt of the 90s and 2000s.Nonetheless, even in classic Hollywood, there was room for variation. The leading men of that era were not carbon copies. Some, like James Stewart, built their careers on a quiet intensity, on a relatable everyman quality. Pitt's ability to embody both rugged masculinity and a certain emotional depth suggests that he could have found a niche, perhaps evolving, as his career progressed, into a character actor, the ultimate chameleon. He could have become one of those faces you instantly recognize, even if his name isn't at the forefront. Perhaps he wouldn't have been the top dog, the matinee idol, but he could certainly have secured a lasting career, perhaps crafting a path slightly different from the trajectory he has thus carved. The question ultimately becomes, not whether, but how.

What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? My most potent epiphany regarding the relentless march of time, the one that truly smacked me in the face and left me reeling, came a few years back. I was idly scrolling through social media, that modern-day hall of mirrors, when I stumbled upon a post about a new television show. Now, I consider myself a relatively informed individual, not impervious to the zeitgeist, yet this show was a complete and utter mystery to me. The title, the actors, the very concept—all foreign and utterly alien. This alone wasn't sufficient to trigger the age alarm bells. My tastes, I reasoned, were simply more...refined. Then, the comments began. People were gushing over the show. "OMG, this is the best thing ever!" one wrote. "I've been waiting for this FOREVER!" another exclaimed. My internal monologue tilted from casual curiosity to a growing sense of unease. These weren't my people, clearly. I went back to my daily life. Later that week I was in a pub, and a group of young men were in the corner, their faces lit by the pale glow of a laptop screen. I peered over there, and they were watching the aforementioned show. My mind boggled. It felt like a completely different language. A new culture had blossomed before my very eyes. Everything else felt ancient and primitive. The show in question? A cartoon about anthropomorphic talking animals. It was then I felt the first tremor of genuine bewilderment and realized, with a sinking heart, that I had become the old man shaking his fist at the clouds. I was well and truly out of the loop. The march of time had finally caught up with me, and I was left staring at a screen thinking what on earth is going on in the damn world.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? This is a question that gnaws at you as the years tick by, isn't it? A constant hum in the background of your life, a little tremor that manifests in various ways. Sometimes it's a pang of envy when you see a friend's overflowing nest, the boisterous chaos of a family Christmas, the way a child's laughter can light up a room. Other times, it's a sigh of relief, a quiet satisfaction with the freedom that childlessness affords: the ability to up sticks and travel at a moment's notice, the financial breathing room, the uninterrupted hours you can devote to hobbies, or simply to staring out the window, lost in thought. You weigh up the pros and cons, the potential joys versus the potential sacrifices (and let's be frank, the potential horrors, too). It's a complex equation, and the answer, if there even *is* a definitive answer, shifts with the tide of your circumstances and your mood.I find myself oscillating between the two extremes. One day I'll be engulfed in a torrent of wistful longing, imagining myself as a doting parent, attending school plays, helping with homework, and imparting my wisdom (however limited) onto the next generation. I romanticize the messy, the overwhelming, the exquisitely exhausting experience of parenthood. Then the next day, I'll be supremely thankful for the peace and quiet, the ability to sleep past eight, the freedom to invest in only myself. And of course, there's the fear -the crushing burden of responsibility, the relentless worries about their health, their happiness, their very survival in this increasingly chaotic and unforgiving world. It can be a terrifying prospect. At the end of the day I suppose I might have the choice to adopt a child however I'm not sure if I will do that. Perhaps my own future depends on the next twist of fate and whatever it may bring.
